description: We are Aurora Rocketeers, an aspiring group of engineers from the Philippines. We aim to use our knowledge in Computer Engineering in making space solutions! 🚀
summary: Project Teraflare is a web-based visualization tool harmonizing the sensor data from MODIS and VIIRS and projecting them on a 3D map of the Earth. Teraflare provides a general overview of the hot spots and statistics of the burning activity from each country. Teraflare provides an interactive and intuitive 3D display of global burning activity that eases the burden on users from taking in too much information displayed from existing burning calendar web applications. Teraflare distinguishes itself from other solutions by also incorporating the average weather conditions, local vegetation, and terrain characteristics of the area in a recognized hot spot which allows emergency responders and land surveyors to have a general idea of the area prone to burning activity.
details:
Project Teraflare is a web-based 3D globe for exploring global burning activity from NASA FIRMS active-fire data. It addresses the challenge’s core problem, that MODIS and VIIRS record fire confidence differently, by mapping both onto one scale in a data pipeline. The globe opens on a clean heat map and adds detail only when the user selects a country, uploads a GeoJSON boundary, or draws a rectangle. The live build explores 17.9 million MODIS detections. VIIRS support and the 2012+ overlap calibration are built into the pipeline and activated as VIIRS files are added. It matters because responders, scientists, and land managers need to see where and when burning concentrates, without the clutter of existing 2D dashboards.

TeraFlare is a 3D globe for exploring global burning activity from NASA FIRMS active-fire data, following a structured, step-by-step flow: (1) overview, a clean global heat map with a time slider; (2) country, region outlines colored by burning frequency plus 3D hexagon columns for top hotspots; and (3) region, the top and lowest burning regions, peak year, busiest month, fire brightness temperature, and yearly and seasonal charts. 

It works like zooming in on a map, from the whole planet to a country to a single neighborhood, where each step adds detail only when the user asks for it. Users can also analyze their own area by uploading a GeoJSON file or drawing a rectangle. The live build explores 17.9 million MODIS detections, and the VIIRS confidence mapping and 2012+ overlap weight are built into the pipeline and switched on when VIIRS files are loaded.

A Python pipeline reads NASA FIRMS CSV files uploaded onto an Azure SQL Databases and maps MODIS confidence (0-100) and VIIRS ratings (low/nominal/high) onto a singular low/nominal/high scale. It bins detections into 0.5° cells by year, sensor, and confidence, and assigns each cell to a country. When both sensors are present, an overlap weight (MODIS detections divided by VIIRS detections, 2012 onward) scales VIIRS counts to MODIS. 

The result is one compact file that the browser downloads once and caches. globe.gl (Three.js/WebGL) draws the heat map and hexagons, and all statistics are computed in the browser. The app runs on Vercel, with Azure as the database and GitHub for version control.

TeraFlare benefits everyone who needs to understand fire, with a clear flow of (1) responders, who can see which regions burn most and in which months, so they know where and when to expect activity; (2) scientists, who get yearly and seasonal patterns on a consistent confidence scale without handling raw CSVs; and (3) land managers, who can analyze their own boundary by GeoJSON or a drawn rectangle, with results under real region and province names. 

It works like a weather forecast for burning activity, where anyone can open it and see at a glance what is likely and where. A clear first view adds detail only on request, and it is free, requires no login, and runs in any modern browser.

TeraFlare is built using the following software tools and languages: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, globe.gl (Three.js/WebGL) with H3 hexagons, Python (NumPy, pandas, Shapely), Vercel, Azure, and GitHub. Everything runs on standard laptops and in any modern browser.

The team wants anyone, not only data specialists, to open a browser and answer: where does this place burn, and when? We built the harmonization into the data pipeline so that adding more satellite records improves the picture without changing the interface.
